author: Lauren Branch
title: Commissioners address need for new fire hydrants in Greenevers - NewsBreak
text:
By Lauren Branch ,
5 hours ago
GREENEVERS — The town is working with the local fire department to conduct a study of fire hydrants in hopes that it will lead to repairs and improve safety and the town’s insurance rating.
Greenevers Fire Department Trainer Lee Kennedy told the Board of Commissioners at their monthly meeting on Nov. 10 that problems exist with 18 of the 55 hydrants in the town’s system. Within those, five hydrants are missing, three hydrants are cut off due to issues and two hydrants were hit and damaged beyond repair.
He referenced an April 2024 fire that killed Morrell Chasen, 88, at his home on Clinic Circle Drive, addressing Mayor Diane Browns and commissioners Venessa Farrior and Gregory Carr specifically.
“Mayor Brown and Commissioner Farrior, right at your house, there should have been a fire hydrant. When your uncle passed and Chief Carr’s uncle passed away, we had to shuttle water, meaning we had to drive to another fire hydrant to get water.
“That took seven or eight people away from that fire scene that could have been helping fight the fire if that hydrant would have been working,” he explained.
Kennedy also works for the Office of the State Fire Marshal, which is responsible for Insurance Services Office (ISO) scores that can impact homeowner and business insurance rates.
“The lower the score the better, so it’s a reverse scale with 10 being the worst and 1 being the best. It’s based off of the fire department, water department, communications center that dispatches and the fire marshal for the county. It’s all a combination of all of those four sections,” he explained.
He stated that there is another state inspection in two years, and he did not want the hydrant issues to affect the town’s score. He believes Brown Terrance Apartments and Pasture Branch Road are both areas that the town needs to focus on because they are highly populated areas.
Commissioner Reginald James asked what it would cost to get the project completed, to which Kennedy responded that it would cost $10,000 to fix two hydrants and $8,000 to fix the one around Brown Terrance Lane.
“Does it depend on how many residents we should have per area around the hydrant?” Farrior asked.
“It’s (a) 1,000-foot buffer around fire hydrants. That’s where you get that reduced rating is that 1,000 foot of a fire hydrant, but we are actually rated based on a water haul program, and that means there’s areas that do not have hydrants, but they still get that break in insurance because we’ve showed that we can produce enough water for that area,” he stated.
He further explained that some homeowners’ insurance companies ask how close a fire hydrant is to their home.
Commissioner Timothy Murphy explained that since there was a variety of issues, some more simple than others, they should put together a list of issues with the cost for each hydrant so that the town could take care of as many issues as they can as soon as possible.
Kennedy explained that near Commissioner Murphy’s house, near Pasture Branch Road, the hydrant had been hit by a bush hog. He recommended that the town have the farmer or the landowner repair it.
Brown thanked Kennedy for coming, stating that the board did not know the issue was as serious as it was.
After a lengthy discussion, the town decided to let the department do a thorough inspection of the hydrants and bring the total project cost to the board.
Other business
Town Administrator Emma Brinson stated that the town was interested in purchasing a membership with NC 811.
“Whenever you are planning to dig, this is the number you need to reach out to that will help locate utilities that may be in the area. Currently the town is not a part of 811, and we would like to join this group so we get locate-requests in a timely manner to help prevent damage to our water and sewer infrastructure,” Brinson explained.
According to Brinson, the membership has a monthly cost, but it should be less than $100. There will also be a cost per call. She believes the town will not need to make many calls since the town does not have a lot of new building projects. Brinson also explained that it is the contractor’s responsibility to call 811.
The board members had several questions and concerns, and the motion was tabled to give the board time to review the information. Mayor Brown also asked Brinson to get an accurate monthly cost.
Brinson also said that Sampson and Duplin counties are requesting feedback on the Sampson-Duplin Regional Hazard Mitigation Plan.
“It looks at all of the towns in Sampson and Duplin County. It’s more like an assessment of our ability to handle different kind of hazards like floods, fires, earthquakes and, of course, hurricanes because we experience those here in Duplin County,” she explained.
The information is posted on the website along with the links to the comment forms and draft plan. Residents are recommended to give their input online.
Brinson stated that the Red Cross reached out about using the community center for short-term disaster relief. After a discussion, the board voted unanimously to approve the partnership.The board voted to apply to the N.C. League of Municipalities to participate in its Municpal Accounting Service Grant Writing program. If the town is chosen, the grants would be written for the town at no cost.Brinson stated that she has received complaints about individuals parking at the community center overnight. The board discussed fixing the broken gate and re-closing the entrances. The discussion was tabled and no vote was taken.Brinson gave the board a copy of a letter sent to residents who live on Hargrove Drive to warn them that a water line extension project will be starting soon and there will be construction in the area. There may be some disruption in service during the work. The project will also allow more residents to receive water who are using private well water.
‘I believe they will start before Thanksgiving,” Brinson said. The engineer is Adams Company and the contractor is T&A Loving. The project should be done by April 2026.
A draft subdivision ordinance remains on hold because the planning board did not meet in October may not meet in November,” Brinson said. Mayor Brown raised a concern about how the delay could impact a property owner planing to place several mobile homes.
“Maybe we need to reach out to that family and let them know that anything we can help them with that subdivision, we want to do it so they can go ahead and get established, because they’ve had those mobile homes there for some time. They’ve already made an investment, so I’m sure they are waiting on a return. Anything we can help with so they can get started, we need to do that,” stated Mayor Brown.
Any individual or organization that is currently working on a project will not be affected by the new ordinance, Brinson said.
Greenevers holds its town board meetings at 7 p.m. on the Monday after the second Sunday at the Greenevers Community Building. All meetings are open to the public.
